items.title: Shitty Screenshare
items.content:
Did you know OBS or FFmpeg can go directly into a video conference? You configure everything,

so you control exactly the quality you are going to get. WHIP support means these tools

now speak the protocol of video conferencing.

Send them an angry email. Tell them you don't want their crappy

proprietary client. You want open standards that let you bring the tools

WHIP is an open standard for sending live video to a service using WebRTC.

Your provider gives you a server URL and a stream key, called a bearer token. Before to join a conference

call each client had to run custom code. That means FFmpeg/OBS would never be able to join.

A lack of control. Your browser is picking a bitrate, codec or resolution that doesn't match what you need.

OBS and FFmpeg let you choose your resolution, frame rate, bitrate, and codec.

You can tune those settings for the content you're sharing and the hardware and connection you have.

OBS Virtual Camera sends your OBS scene to the conferencing app as a webcam.

You can pick the layout of your stream, but the conferencing app still handles encoding.

See the OBS WHIP setup guide I try and keep it up to date.

I work on WHIP in OBS. I'm tired of shitty screenshares when it is easily fixed.
items.title_ko: OBS·FFmpeg를 WHIP으로 화상회의에 직접 연결하기
items.summary_ko: OBS와 FFmpeg는 WHIP 지원을 통해 화상회의에 직접 영상을 보낼 수 있게 되었다. 이를 통해 해상도, 프레임 레이트, 비트레이트, 코덱을 사용자가 직접 설정할 수 있다. 글쓴이는 WHIP을 OBS에 구현하는 작업을 하고 있다.
items.content_ko: OBS나 FFmpeg를 화상회의에 바로 연결할 수 있다는 점을 알고 있는가. WHIP 지원 덕분에 이 도구들은 화상회의에서 쓰는 프로토콜로 영상을 보낼 수 있다. WHIP은 WebRTC를 이용해 라이브 영상을 서비스로 보내는 개방형 표준이다. 서비스 제공자는 서버 URL과 스트림 키(베어러 토큰)를 준다. 기존에는 회의에 참여하려면 각 클라이언트가 전용 코드를 실행해야 했고, 그래서 FFmpeg나 OBS는 참여할 수 없었다. 브라우저는 필요한 것과 다른 비트레이트, 코덱, 해상도를 고를 수 있어 통제력이 부족하다. OBS와 FFmpeg에서는 해상도, 프레임 레이트, 비트레이트, 코덱을 직접 고를 수 있으며, 공유하는 콘텐츠와 장비, 연결 환경에 맞춰 조정할 수 있다. OBS 가상 카메라는 OBS 장면을 회의 앱에 웹캠으로 보낸다. 스트림 레이아웃은 정할 수 있지만 인코딩은 여전히 회의 앱이 맡는다. 글쓴이는 OBS WHIP 설정 가이드를 최신 상태로 관리하고 있다고 적었다. 본문은 중간에 끊겨 있다.

items.title: ICE plan to buy robot dogs spurs protest from hundreds of Boston Dynamics employees
items.content:
Boston Dynamics' Spot robot walks around during a demonstration at company's facility in Waltham in 2024. (Josh Reynolds/AP)

Dozens of Boston Dynamics employees are calling on the company to stop the sale of its AI-powered robot dogs to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Known as "Spot," Boston Dynamics' robots are dog-like autonomous machines with four legs that can climb stairs and do backflips. They're equipped with cameras and sensors.

The company faced some backlash in late August, when it was first revealed that the Department of Homeland Security planned to purchase the robots . A  $1.3 million contract with ICE was settled in September for the sale of four robot dogs and other Spot technology.

Employees wrote in a petition , obtained by WBUR and sent in early September to company leadership, that the sale hurts Boston Dynamics' image and "presents us as working directly with ICE" as the agency has "worked to sow fear" across the country.

A Boston Dynamics spokesperson confirmed the petition Friday, but said "nearly half" of its 300 signatures were entered as "Anonymous." The company employs more than 1,500 people.

"We cannot be proud of working at [Boston Dynamics] when that work is being used by a government agency that brutalizes civilians, including some of our own colleagues ... ," the petition read.

ICE previously said the robots would give them an additional safety tool that can "provide real-time situational awareness in hazardous, confined, or tactically uncertain environments" before agents are sent to a scene. The agency had added the robot dogs wouldn't replace "human judgment" from its law enforcement officers.

Boston Dynamics argues the dogs are being sold to ICE's Homeland Security Investigations unit, which primarily focuses on transnational criminal matters — not removal operations.

But Boston Dynamics employees said in the letter that the risk to the company is "too great to continue with this deal," adding it could cause staffers to quit or turn away potential new hires.

"Our public-facing teams have received external emails concerned about this deal," the petition read. "Many of us have gotten messages from friends and family, asking us in disbelief and horror if this news is true, and how we can live with ourselves if it is."

In a letter to employees, Boston Dynamics interim CEO Amanda McMaster wrote that after considering the petition, the company is standing by its decision to sell the robots to ICE.

McMaster said customers must comply with the company's terms and conditions for sale, which "prohibit any attempts to weaponize our robot or use it for purposes of harm or intimidation."

"I ask you to respect and accept this decision, even if you do not agree with it," McMaster wrote.

The company's  ethical principles state "if our products are being used for harm, we will take appropriate measures to mitigate that misuse." However, it's unclear what those mitigation measures would be.

'Spot'으로 불리는 이 로봇은 계단을 오르고 뒤공중제비를 할 수 있는 네 다리 자율주행 기계로, 카메라와 센서를 갖췄다. 8월 말 국토안보부(DHS)가 이 로봇을 구매하려 한다는 사실이 처음 알려지며 반발이 일었다. items.title: CSS-Tricks has a new owner
items.content:
NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle.

This is pretty wild, but let’s get right to it because it’s big news:

CSS-Tricks is an independent site once again!

Just to recap:  DigitalOcean purchased CSS-Tricks in 2022  from Chris Coyier, who founded the site in 2007. Chris ran it all the way up to that purchase.

Here we are in 2026, and I’m taking independent ownership of the site.

So, wait, who owns the site? That’d be me. (Wow, never imagined I would get to say that!) Of course, I have  a small, awesome team  to help with the day-to-day management of the site.

That all said, I do envision that some things will change. In fact, I’m planning that they will change in what I hope are very good ways. Maybe a question-answer thing makes sense here since this is very much an evolving discussion.

Yes, I’ve got the keys to the castle, so to speak. And, even after 12 years of working on the site, I’ll admit I’m a little overwhelmed and nervous about that. I mean, it’s an investment for sure, as you can imagine, and I’m making this my full-time job. At least for a while.

I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of  everyone , no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time.

My latest IPO launched, and I’m now worth one trillion dollars. Wait, wait. That’s not right.

It’s going to be hard. Advertising will certainly be needed now. But, in order to keep the lights on, I’ll have to approach them differently.

In the pre-DigitalOcean days we sold real ad packages with things like display ads, sponsored posts, newsletter sponsors, and the like. As an independent website, we will need to return to our advertising roots.

So, if you’re in a place looking to advertise,  please do reach out !

Right?! Ad revenue can’t be the only thing paying the bills. I have lots of ideas and several plates already spinning. Like, I’ve been neck deep in developing an HTML/CSS course for beginners.

(And you can now support the site by becoming a member  — thanks in advance!)

Educational content has been in the dumps lately, right? Again, I’m hoping that CSS-Tricks will be more inclusive, no matter where you or anyone else is at in the learning journey. This place has traditionally been for folks who know what they’re doing. But I’m truly committed to creating more entry points for those getting started, particularly as  our field is in the early throes of a growing skills gap .

And yes, I do believe that  learning the basics is more important now than ever . But what learning actually looks like is what’s key. Front-end courses are  down across the board . It has to be done differently.

There are other things in the works, but I think a course is one of the first things you’ll see.

Oh, and  the newsletter . That’s coming back after a way-too-long hiatus.

That’s still very much a thing! We’ll keep our regularly scheduled broadcast going.

But maybe a little less than you’re used to. Those articles are part of the investment I’m making. Expect maybe one or two articles most weeks, at least as the ball starts rolling.

That also means the  guest writing form  is back in business! We have a nice backlog of articles through the rest of the year, which is great, but also means new submissions will have to wait a bit.

I won’t be able to accept everything that comes in, but I will absolutely read them and follow-up as best I can.  Unless it’s a slop submission , of course.

Will you be writing most of the articles to save cost?

Nah! My goal is to make CSS-Tricks a platform that gives folks a voice to share great ideas. I think we all prefer that over me just using it as my own soapbox. I’ve written plenty for this site the past 12 years. I’m happier (and more comfortable) being behind the curtain and giving others the full spotlight.

I may be writing a bit, developing the site here and there, editing a small stack of article drafts, or…

items.content_ko: Chris Coyier는 DigitalOcean이 2022년 인수했던 CSS-Tricks가 다시 독립 사이트가 되었다고 알렸습니다. 2007년 사이트를 개설한 그는 인수 전까지 직접 운영했으며, 이번에 사이트의 소유자가 되었다고 밝혔습니다. 12년간 사이트에서 일해 왔음에도 이 책임이 부담스럽고 긴장된다고 말하면서, 이를 당분간 전업으로 맡을 계획이라고 전했습니다. 소규모 팀이 일상 관리를 돕고 있으며, 사이트에는 여러 변화가 있을 예정입니다. 질의응답 형식을 도입하는 것도 고려 중입니다. 목표는 진정한 커뮤니티이면서 모든 사람을 포용하는 공간을 만드는 것입니다.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: AI training platform Outlier illegally surveils European platform workers
items.content:
Today, noyb (in collaboration with  Intérêt à Agir ,  DIPLab and  Reversing.Works ) has filed 5 complaints against Scale AI in France, Italy, the Netherlands and Austria. The US-based company operates an AI training platform named Outlier, which employs more than 900,000 “freelance” workers. Among its customers: Meta, OpenAI, Google – and the US government. However, it's not just the workers' extensive knowledge and experience that Scale AI is farming: The company collects huge amounts of personal data and forces workers to go through an invasive biometric verification to earn money. In Europe, this far-reaching workplace surveillance clearly violates the workers’ fundamental right to data protection.

Complaint in Austria #1 ; Complaint in Austria #2

Report by DiPLab on workplace surveillance by AI training platforms

What is platform work – and what does it have to do with AI? From courier services like Uber and food delivery services, all the way to data annotation:  more than 40 million people already  have their work organised by platforms. This puts people in a vulnerable position: Among other things, companies try to circumvent labour laws by (wrongly) claiming that their workers are self-employed. This often excludes them from social benefits  and affects their wages . Unsurprisingly, the AI industry heavily relies on this new type of work. Popular AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok are also trained by actual people who manually review or annotate their output.

Scale AI – almost 1 million workers. One of the  biggest players in this field is the US company Scale AI, which operates the data annotation platform Outlier AI. Outlier employs more than 900,000 “freelance” platform workers who train AI systems by solving tasks (e.g. writing prompts, ranking answers, etc.), effectively giving their expert knowledge to US Big Tech companies. Its  best-known customers are  corporations such as Meta, OpenAI, xAI, Google, Anthropic,  and the US government .

Thomas Le Bonniec, sociology researcher at DIPLab: “Platform work seems to be fertile ground for a whole new type of workplace surveillance. This would be seen as unacceptable in any other form of employment in the European Union. This system only thrives because of its deliberate lack of transparency.”

Invasive tracking. However, questionable employment practices are not the only issue: Outlier is subjecting its workers to invasive tracking. Our technical analysis showed that while workers are on the Outlier platform, trackers from companies such as TikTok, LinkedIn, Facebook, the survey platform Sprig and the data analysis company Datadog are placed on their devices. Every few seconds, these trackers send the workers’ personal data to third parties. This includes IP addresses, contact details, unique identifiers and information about the visited page. Among other things, this data can then be used for targeted advertising and profiling.

Lisa Steinfeld Leiser, Data Protection Lawyer at noyb : “Such constant and extensive trackingwhile working really goes against all reasonable expectations. Why should LinkedIn or Facebook know which tasks you're working on?”

Forced biometric identification. As if that weren’t enough, Scale AI also forces workers to repeatedly go through a biometric verification process carried out by a company called Persona. This includes video recordings of their face and uploading their ID. Scale AI claims that this is done to prevent identity fraud and to “verify the workers’ skills” . In reality, this not only goes far beyond what would be necessary, but Persona also has a questionable history when it comes to data security. In October 2025, approximately 70,000 photos of government issued IDs stored with Persona  were exposed by hackers . On top of that, Persona grants itself the right to collect heaps of personal data, including IP addresses, device information, geolocation data, addresses, and consumer credit data of users.

items.title: 대기업 총수, 의장 경제문제 때문에 못조져 놓는다는 건
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

마치 테러리스트가 인질극 벌이는데 인질 죽는다고 테러리스트 진압 안하겠다는 것과 같은 말이다.

총수, 의장 검찰 총원해서 조져 놓다가 사면을 해놓으니까 버릇이 안좋아 진건지 아니면 반도체좀 했다고 뭐가 된양인지 모르겠다만

앞으로 대한민국에서도 여당과 야당 합작으로 대기업 총수, 의장 사법처리하고 사면하지않고 만기 출소하는 케이스가 단 한 번이라도 나와서 명확하게 그 선례를 남겨놔야한다는게 내 생

items.title: Sebastian Raschka's from-scratch video course on building reasoning models
items.content:
Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course

Eight videos and over 11 hours of coding, covering evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation in Python and PyTorch.

I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode.

For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work.

Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content).

We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite).

I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along!

How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together

As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos.

A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well.

A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools.

Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article.

In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.)

So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents.

The resources accompanying these topics shown above are:

The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos

The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below)

The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack

The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system.

The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation.

items.title: A faster way to compute signed 64-bit floor division by constants
items.content:
Signed integer floor division is where you do a/b and get a result that rounds towards − ∞ ,

whereas standard ( “truncated” ) signed division rounds towards 0 .

As stated in Hacker's Delight: “[I suspect that] floor division more often gives the result you want” .

This article is about floor division where the divisor is known at compile time .

Despite the usefulness of this function, the world of integer floor division is in shambles:

This blog post aims to not only shine light on the fast algorithms, but will also introduce a new fast approach which, with ideal compilation:

The benchmark section has a detailed overview showing per-divisor results over many platforms, for throughput and latency.

It works in all bit-widths, and may find use on some 32-bit or SIMD applications, but the biggest benefit is in 64-bit.

It also can be used for faster positive-modulus, and faster "Euclidean" division (differs to floor division for negative divisors) .

Floor division can be much faster than you probably realise.

Below is a snapshot throughput benchmark for division by 86400 (the number of seconds in one day) , the kind of performance you can expect using most languages' built-in methods, vs fast alternatives outlined in this blog.

Floor Div 86400 throughput - ARM64 Chips As tested on MacBook Pro M4 Pro

Floor Div 86400 throughput - X86 Chips As tested on AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D

*Rust provides "div_euclid", which matches floor-div for positive divisors.

See the benchmark section for a deeper comparison across over 40 divisors.

For the avoidance of doubt, the license only applies if you copy/paste the comment and code verbatim. No license is required if you re-write the same logic in your code.

A set of 65535 divisors from -32768 to 32767 for 64-bit can be generated into a single self-contained C++ file. It includes a boundary test in the same file.

See the comment at the top of the download for how to build and run it.

Using this form, you can choose any bit-width and any divisor to get a copy/paste function ready to go.

There is also reference algorithm (a reusable C++ template with additional microarchitectural performance tweaks) .

As you can see, the technique is so simple that I'd expect that somebody has done this before, but I've looked around and not found it documented anywhere. If it turns out to have been done before, at least this page will make it discoverable.

For the rest of us, I'll cover a narrative about floor division, which matches my process of discovery... And if you want to create a fast library or compiler/language implementation, this will be your one-stop shop.

items.title: I guess I’m using WebP now?
items.content:
After using the same few image formats for 20+ years, I’m now on the WebP bandwagon. That isn’t something I thought I’d ever say. Now I’m wondering how soon it’ll be before I can use a couple more.

When Google announced the WebP format in 2010 it was interesting, but only academically. WebP support was added to Chrome in 2011 , 1 but other browsers took their time supporting it: Edge in 2018 , Firefox in 2019 , and Safari in 2020 . Until there was baseline support , the format was only being used selectively by content delivery networks . Even then, WebP was a pain to work with. Photoshop didn’t get native support until 2022 , and its “ Save for Web ” and “ Export As ” features still don’t support the format.

Because of all this, I found WebP annoying. I wasn’t alone, either . Things weren’t helped by Google’s eagerness to push the format. Their Lighthouse tool would often complain that images weren’t in WebP , even when file size savings were relatively minor and format support was immature. For the past 20+ years, I’ve only really used JPEGs , PNGs , and (later) SVGs to serve images on the web. 2

Since ditching Photoshop for Pixelmator Pro, I now have much nicer tooling for dealing with WebP images. It turns out they’re pretty good? In the past two Liquid Glass grumble-pieces , I used WebPs because they were smaller than JPEGs or PNGs at the same visual quality. This won’t always be the case, but I’ve not yet encountered a situation where WebP doesn’t come out on top. Google has some findings on this for lossy and lossless versions of WebP.

It’s not very surprising that WebP has advantages over JPEG or PNG. Even when I found the format annoying, I knew there were benefits. The difference is that I no longer have to go out of my way to use the format. Now I’m wondering if/when newer standards like JPEG XL or AVIF will be supported by Pixelmator Pro. AVIF in particular looks very promising to me, and it also has baseline support across browsers . Just a few days ago, Google announced it was shipping JPEG XL support , 3 so that might hit baseline in the near future as well.

I’m certainly not as annoyed by AVIF or JPEG XL. Hopefully I won’t have to wait as long to easily take advantage of them.

GIFs were also around, but only really for memes. Now they’re usually transformed into much smaller videos . I last used GIFs on the regular when I was laying things out with tables .  ↩

After having dropped it not too long ago . Google’s gonna Google.  ↩

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Former Yahoo CEO Needed AI to Help Describe What Makes Her Own Daughter Special
items.content:
Marissa Mayer, the original Silicon Valley girlboss, is back with a new artificial intelligence tool specifically for moms. Specifically, moms who don’t really like doing mom stuff.

In a profile of Mayer and her new AI assistant, called Dazzle , the New York Times provided an anecdote , presumably passed on to the reporter by Mayer herself, to highlight how this agent has made her life easier—though, if anything, it shows Mayer performing the exact kind of cognitive offloading that any AI tool worth its salt should free us up to focus on rather than doing for us.

Per The Times, Mayer said that she was asked by her daughter’s teacher to come up with three things that make her daughter special as part of a celebration of her daughter’s 10th birthday. Mayer, apparently feeling overwhelmed by the task, asked Dazzle to do it for her. “It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover,” Mayer told the Times . Surely, her daughter will appreciate learning that an AI model scraped through her mom’s photos of her to come up with those because her mom couldn’t be bothered.

That is the catch with Dazzle—instead of asking for full access to a user’s texts, emails, and documents the way most AI agents do, Mayer’s assistant goes after a person’s photos.

“Your camera roll is the ultimate personal context,” the company explains on its landing page . “Every photo you take holds rich context about your preferences, style, hobbies, loved ones, and everyday tasks. Dazzle transforms your camera into a proactive assistant that understands you, what you need help with, and what you like.”

Communicating with the AI agent works the same way. Instead of typing a prompt and getting a response, Dazzle has users snap a photo as the starting point and lets the agent point to what it thinks the next course of action should be. “Snap a picture of a purchase you’ve been thinking about, a flat tire, or fridge ingredients, and Dazzle buys on approval, schedules repairs, or suggests recipes,” the company says.

That’s… fine? It’s unclear that it’s fundamentally different from most AI assistants, which also can snag information from an image, but Mayer’s whole schtick seems to be “AI for women,” and by her estimation, photos are more girly while text prompts are for boys. “Women, this is my own bias, tend to take more photos and are more visual, and so being able to work with A.I. in a visual medium is fun,” Mayer told the Times .

Mayer isn’t wrong that women have basically been left behind by AI. The vast majority of people who built the technology are men, imposing their biases—consciously and unconsciously—onto everything from the training data to how AI models communicate and how people interact with them. Studies have shown that AI models have a gender bias problem , producing misogynistic and sexist outputs, and women have thus far been less likely to engage with AI than men.

But the solution surely isn’t a pink coat of paint and a girlypop attitude. At one point in the Times piece, the publication suggests that “maybe what overextended professional women need is an A.I. wife, an emotional labor bot.” And…you see the problem here, right? That in trying to address a problem in part created by gender biases, we are leaning into those very same misogynistic tropes and saying the woman (or woman-shaped bots) should do emotional labor for us? Like, did we think about this for more than a second?

A daily briefing on the AI news you need to know to start your day. Written by humans. Envied by bots.

In the scheme of things, Dazzle is mostly just another AI tool that wants to hyper-target its users and help them buy more stuff, with little in the way of actual solutions for the kind of monotonous stuff that eats up a person’s time and energy.

If you want an AI agent to buy shoes for you because you just don’t have the energy to do it yourself, fine. But please don’t use AI to figure out what is special about your kid.…

Lots of porting work has happened this release. The Wasm feature is now enabled by default, so Wild

can be used to link Wasm with the caveat that debug info isn't yet supported.

Support for GNU linker scripts is greatly enhanced. Wild now supports enough of the linker script

syntax that it can link Linux kernel modules and is close to being able to link the Linux kernel

The Mac port has made significant progress. The feature isn't yet to the point where we're prepared

to enable it by default, but Wild is able to link itself on Mac and at least one of the maintainers

is now using Wild as their default linker for Rust on Mac.

We've also fixed some performance issues that were affecting various filesystems and made a few

general performance improvements. We also got a bit slower due to implementing proper ELF COMDAT

We now cap the number of threads to at most 32 unless overridden by --threads. This avoids bad

performance that occurs with larger numbers of threads due to contention on a Linux per-inode mutex.

Our benchmarks have been expanded to include a wider range of scenarios such as different

filesystems and whether the output file already exists.

items.title: Websites Should Be Printable
items.content:
If you have questions or thoughts on the post I'd love to hear about it!

I'm currently looking for work in the northeastern US. I'll be graduating with a BS in both Computer Science and Cyber Operations at the end of the school year.

I have worked in web application development and Java, and I have experience in Rust, C++, Python, and various other languages.

If you're curious about what I've done in the past, I keep up a short list of projects here or contact me to give me a place to send my resume.

I figure anyone who reads my posts will have an interesting offer, so all leads are appreciated!

I read a lot of printed papers these days. While I enjoy reading on a laptop as much as the next guy, marking up a printed document engages me better. Also, there's something about sitting with a whiteboard and a printed document that makes me rightly feel like I'm doing something important. So I've been thinking about how to best allow others to enjoy this medium for content that I write.

Luckily for me, printed documents were a major focus of web design a while ago. You can print any webpage you like, by hitting CTRL-P and hoping your printer driver decides to cooperate today.

I tested this on my own webpage, foolishly thinking I would have a decent print job without any effort.

It wasn't great, although you can at least see all the content. The text was too big by about 2 levels, the header looks awful when printed, and my links look awfully gray in black-and-white. Totally unacceptable.

Luckily, the web community has had this aforementioned focus on printing documents from HTML pages. CSS has selectors to allow styling specifically printed content, and they can be useful. Here's my print-related snippet for this page now:

You can see the effects of this snippet by hitting CTRL-P or the print button on this page. Here's the functions this does for me, in order:

After attempting to optimize my website in this way, I am sympathetic for those who wouldn't prioritize printing. Hiding and showing all the right things in print took me a decent chunk of my morning. My site isn't very complex. I also doubt how many people regularly print webpages out. I might be the only one.

Still, if all your website consists of is text, allowing people to experience the text in their favorite medium is never a bad thing. The digital medium allows a lot of flexibility. The road to good software is paved with kindnesses from software engineers to their users. One day, perhaps someone shall find this kindness and smile, even if just for a fleeting moment. And that will be worth it.

Edit 2026-10-26: I was informed by a friend that this post ended up on the front page of HN and lobste.rs after I submitted it. Fun! Despite the several flaws I am now informed of in my CSS, I hope this article at least pushes a few to consider this medium more carefully. Thanks all for reading!

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Top Economist Finds That AI Has Provided “Zero Financial Payoff” to Companies Outside Tech: "There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth."
items.content:
Over the weekend, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk issued a stark warning : investing in AI cloud computing companies is ill-advised and could result in “guppy-level death and consolidation.”

Analysts have been raising concerns that leading hyperscaler CoreWeave could soon collapse under its own weight, pointing out that it’s taken on over $50 billion in debt, while burning through cash at an alarming rate.

It’s a familiar line of thinking as fears of the AI bubble bursting continue to haunt investors, a potentially doomsday-level economic event that could send ripples across the entire global economy .

And despite the enormous amounts of money that keep being poured in, an actual return on investments remains a distant dream. One major reality check, as Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok argued in a note over the weekend : outside of the tech industry, AI has yet to deliver on any meaningful economic advantages for businesses — amounting to what he called “zero financial payoff.”

“Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493,” he wrote. “Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493,” adding that “there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth.”

It’s the latest vote of no confidence as fears of a colossal money pit caving in on itself continue to grow. Much of corporate America has struggled to see much in the way of the promised benefits that are directly reflected on their balance sheets.

“The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector,” Slok concluded.

Worse yet, the costs to make use of frontier models have soared, forcing companies to switch to cheaper solutions. Besides, whether firms can actually benefit from highly sophisticated tech that can identify cybersecurity threats with ease or autonomously hack a third party’s servers remains a glaring question.

“Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins,” Slok wrote.

Despite having just announced a half a billion dollar AI push, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon told investors last week that “there’s very little that we do where we need frontier models,” as Fortune reports .

The “bigger-picture frontier issues that are getting a lot of attention” are “really separate from using the base tools that exist to support your businesses,” Solomon argued.

Meanwhile, the AI industry is being majorly tested this week, with Anthropic officially filing to go public. But the fact that it blew through a staggering $80.7 billion in just the first half of this year could exacerbate fears as business leaders ponder whether the juice really is worth the squeeze.

More on the AI industry: IMF Warns That AI Bubble Could Take Down the Entire World Economy

items.title: Oldest GUI application that still runs on Windows 11
items.content:
For a while I’ve been wondering about a silly question, which is, what’s the oldest application with a GUI that will still run on Windows 11 without modifications or emulation.

Given Windows’ excellent backwards compatibility, I expected the answer to be something impressively old.

Sadly, Windows 11 can’t run 16-bit Windows programs by itself, because 64-bit Windows has no NTVDM , so we’re going to have to find something from the early NT era.

I remember asking this question a while ago on an anonymous forum, where someone pointed me to Win32s , and suggested to find an early release version of it with FREECELL.exe .

So I did exactly that, and lo and behold, FREECELL.EXE with a date modified of 22-Feb-93 running and fully playable, without any changes on the latest version of Windows 11:

At the time of this post, that’s a 33 years and 8 months old application, which is impressively almost as old as me.

So I kinda thought “cool”, considered this a solved mystery and forgot about it shortly afterwards. But for some reason, this question popped into my mind again lately and this time I decided to dig deeper to see if I can find something older.

Digging through old Windows versions on the Internet Archive, I found some early NT 3.1 pre-release versions that seemed promising, but the main issue seemed to be either incompatibility with today’s executable format or API changes that came later in development.

The earliest 1991 versions used a draft PE format not compatible with modern Windows, and builds up to mid-1992 assumed the cdecl calling convention instead of stdcall for Windows API calls, so arguments would get removed twice, as such:

call [ShowWindow] ; Win11 ShowWindow is stdcall, ends with "ret 4" and removes them

add esp, 4 ; the 1992 caller removes them again

Which would understandably cause the program to crash.

There was one application that caught my eye though, from Build 347, and that was CDPLAYER.EXE , linked on 16-Nov-1992 . By then the calling convention was fixed, but the other programs in that build crash in their bundled C runtime. CDPLAYER.EXE avoids that by using the system’s crtdll.dll , and Windows 11 still ships a crtdll.dll in SysWOW64 .

If you start the program, you get something like this:

That is because, duh, my computer doesn’t have a CD-ROM drive. But you can use a small DLL ( cdemu.dll ) to emulate one with some fake audio data and actually get it to play audio:

Pretty cool for a program that’s almost 34 years old!

So earlier I mentioned that 16-bit programs are out of the picture because they are no longer supported.

But if you want, you can use something like otvdm to run older Windows applications.

Behold, a fully playable version of REVERSI.EXE dated 15-Nov-1985 running on Windows 11, taken from Windows 1.01:

And although using otvdm does feel like cheating, I thought it was cool enough to include in this post.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: AI models cost more when you don’t use English: Some languages require far more tokens for AI models to process, raising costs and reducing context for the people who use them.
items.content:
People who use less widely spoken languages could end up paying more to use artificial intelligence than those who speak English or other dominant languages.

A new study published last month by the Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research found AI models require far more tokens for some languages than others. Tokens are the units of text or data that the models process. The researchers have called this a hidden “tokenizer tax,” which can make AI more expensive in languages with smaller online presence. A tokenizer is a tool that breaks down raw text, images, or audio into tokens.

Tokenization example. A graphic representation of the tokenization of the sentence “People should benefit from AI, regardless of the language they speak.”in English and Malayalam using The OpenAI tokenizer API (https://platform.openai.com/tokenizer) . The English sentence gets split into recognizable words, while the Malayalam sentence gets multiple fragments per word without respect for multi-byte characters.

Even within the 20 most popular languages on the internet, there is a gap in token usage, the research found. The most expensive of the languages used between 1.5 and 5 times more tokens than the cheapest. This gap widened when researchers expanded the set to 200 languages, with the token cost gap in one AI model growing by 17 times.

“A startup in [Bengaluru] may pay a surcharge on every prompt and completion while its competitor in Austin does not,” the study said. “The tokenizer tax also has implications beyond cost. Higher token counts translate into higher latency and reduced effective context capacity. These penalties hit hardest where compute and connectivity are already limited. Tokenizer inequity is a constraint on who can participate in the AI economy.”

Non-English languages leave less room for documents or conversation history, and require more work to generate the answer, according to Pratyush Choudhury, co-founder of Activate AI, India’s first venture capital fund dedicated exclusively to AI. Activate backs multilingual voice AI startups like ElevenLabs, Sarvam, and Wispr Flow.

“Think about a tutor: Retaining the student’s earlier mistakes and explanations is part of delivering a good lesson. If that history consumes the context window much faster in one language, the disadvantage reaches into the quality of the service,” he said.

One way to improve language processing is to improve the underlying data.

“Open data efforts matter here, like RESPIN, a collaborative initiative with [the Indian Institute of Science] funded by the Gates Foundation, where we collected text from native speakers of 38 dialects along with read speech,” Raoul Nanavati, co-founder and CEO of Mumbai-based AI voice infrastructure startup Navana.ai , told Rest of World .

However, the study by the Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research found the rarity of a language isn’t the only determinant of how many tokens it uses. The script plays a big role.

Asturian, which has relatively few speakers and no Common Crawl data , “benefits from the Latin-script advantage, as well as the representation from other related Romance languages like Italian,” while languages written in scripts the tokenizer rarely saw — Burmese, Tibetan, Tifinagh, Khmer, Lao, and Ol Chiki — were at the greatest disadvantage consistently across nearly all models in the analysis.

Many tokenizers today remain disproportionately optimized for English and other high-resource languages, and the underlying issue is the lack of high-quality digital data, said Dheemanth Reddy, CEO of Maya Research, which is d eveloping conversational AI models designed to speak and respond like native speakers for the next 5 billion internet users . But better training data alone doesn’t fix the tokenizer, he warned.

items.title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
items.content:
Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Photograph: China News Service/Getty Images

Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Photograph: China News Service/Getty Images

Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll

Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom

Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.

The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.

The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.

AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.

US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies

The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.

The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.

The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.

“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.

The US has banned humanoid robots from China , citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.

As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.

But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.

Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.

“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.

items.content_ko: 베이징은 로보틱스(체화형 AI, embodied AI)를 AI를 사회 전반에 확산시키는 핵심으로 보고 투자를 더 늘리고 있습니다. 그러나 수익성 부족과 서방 국가들의 위협으로 베이징 AI 붐의 지속 가능성에 대한 우려가 커지고 있습니다. STAR 50 지수는 6월 이후 40% 급락했고, 주요 다른 지수들도 같은 기간 약 20% 하락했습니다. 블룸버그에 따르면 5월 이후 중국 증시에서 사라진 금액은 2.4조 달러이며, 골드만삭스는 AI 관련주가 중국과 홍콩 시장 가치의 40% 이상을 차지한다고 분석했습니다. 본문은 중간에서 끊겨 있습니다.

items.title: 의뢰 맡깁니다
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Why is it so expensive to send an email?
items.content:
Why is it so expensive to send an email?

Sending an email is essentially the same as making an HTTPS request. You open a TCP connection to port 25, you do a little SSL handshake, and you send some data through. Most personal computers out there can easily do this thousands of times per second, so how can companies charge $15 to send 1000 emails?! Why do I need some 3rd party company involved at all?! I used to work at Google specifically on GMail, and nothing from my little corner of the product on the “tabbed inbox” team led me to a clear answer...

Unfortunately for me, I was determined to figure it out for myself!

I mostly program with Haskell, and I call C code as necessary for things like OpenSSL and SQLite. I already had a setup for making HTTPS requests from my Haskell code with OpenSSL. I had code for working with HTTP 1.1 messages. How hard could it be to adapt this to email? To my surprise, it turns out that the actual “sending” part is not that hard. The real problem was ultimately out of my hands...

Just like the original plaintext Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP 1.1), there is a correspondingly goofy plaintext protocol for sending emails called Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP). The original version of the protocol involves sending a bunch of messages back and forth and back and forth between the sender and receiver. It looks kind of like a little conversation. Here is an example where I start my messages with keywords like HELO and MAIL FROM and the receiver starts her messages with status codes like 220 and 250 :

250 Hello evancz.dev, I am glad to meet you

From: "Evan from Elm" <devnull@evancz.dev>

To: "Alice from Cryptography" <alice@example.com>

I loved your collaboration with Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman

in 1977. I have been eagerly awaiting the invention of email,

so that I could express my admiration through this plaintext

So to send a single email, you originally had to do SEVEN roundtrips! And TLS did not exist at that time, so you did not even get any encryption after all those roundtrips!

That said, it is not that hard to send and receive a bunch of goofy plaintext, so I set it up and sent an email to myself. It worked! But... it showed up in spam.

The original protocol has a very serious flaw. How does mail.example.com know that I am devnull@evancz.dev and not an imposter? The original protocol lets you just claim whatever sender you want, so anybody in the whole world could easily spoof the domain and sender.

So these days you need to add some TXT records to the DNS for your domain. This way the receiver can go look up some public encryption keys for evancz.dev and confirm that whoever sent the email at least has access to the private key.

At this point I started wondering, wait, how do you prevent someone from spoofing the DNS records? Like what if the NSA and AT&T were collaborating or what if the CIA had a history of creating companies like Crypto AG to backdoor cryptographic systems from the very beginning ? It seems like a problem... But hey, I just want to send an email and it looks like all you have to do is set up these DNS records.

So I set up a private key, added some DNS records, ran my emails through some OpenSSL functions, and I started sending emails again!

Now my emails were showing up in my inbox in GMail! Heck yeah! The technical details were not hard, only sort of annoying to figure out. So why does it cost $15 to send 1000 emails?!

When the database backend for Elm went into private alpha, I decided to try sending the transactional emails myself. Just some Haskell and C code making TCP connections! My thinking was that if I ever set up a hosting service to support Elm development, maybe it would be cool to handle emails as well. The whole goal of Elm is to filter out all the irrelevant details and let the programmer focus on the actually meaningful parts, so it seemed like there might be something there!

items.title_ko: 이메일 발송 비용은 왜 이렇게 비쌀까?
items.summary_ko: 작성자는 이메일 발송이 사실상 HTTPS 요청과 비슷해 기술적으로 어렵지 않다고 보았지만, 실제 장벽은 자신의 통제 밖에 있었다고 말합니다. 일반 PC로 초당 수천 번 연결할 수 있는데도 1,000통에 15달러를 받는 이유를 파고드는 글입니다. 작성자는 Haskell로 SMTP 발송 코드를 직접 만들어 보며 그 원인을 찾으려 했습니다.
items.content_ko: 작성자는 이메일 발송이 사실상 HTTPS 요청과 같다고 보고, 왜 1,000통에 15달러를 받는지 질문을 던집니다. 과거 Google에서 GMail 팀 일부로 일했지만 탭형 받은편지함(tabbed inbox) 팀에서는 명확한 답을 찾지 못했다고 말합니다. 작성자는 주로 Haskell로 프로그래밍하며, OpenSSL과 SQLite 같은 C 코드를 필요에 따라 호출한다고 소개합니다. 이미 OpenSSL로 HTTPS 요청을 보내는 코드와 HTTP 1.1 메시지 처리 코드가 있어, 이를 이메일에 적용해 보려 했다고 설명합니다. 실제로 메일을 보내는 부분은 생각보다 어렵지 않았다고 합니다. 평문 프로토콜인 SMTP에 대한 설명이 이어지지만 본문이 중간에서 끊겨 있습니다.

items.title: Solar power is becoming bigger than nuclear
items.content:
'It's offensively cheap': How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear

1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google

After defying projections, solar's dramatic growth means it is now overtaking nuclear as a global power source. Here are seven reasons for solar's success, and where it might go from here.

The world's solar power is crossing a threshold. A decade ago, it barely registered on a global scale, providing just 1% of the world's power. In 2026, it will almost certainly increase to 10% of power, and overtake nuclear, a mainstay of electricity since the late 1970s.

Globally, solar electricity generation quietly overtook nuclear power (just) in 2025, according to statistics from UK-based energy think tank Ember . And BBC analysis of Ember data over  the past 12 months up to September 2026 shows it clearly outstripping nuclear, producing 13% more power.

"[Solar] generating more electricity than all the world's nuclear power plants is a pretty insane stat, for sure," says Dave Jones, co-founder of Ember.

From China's vast arrays to a recent solar upsurge driven by escalating oil prices, the incredible rise of solar power has defied all projections. Here are seven ways it has become an apparently "unstoppable force" – and what the future looks like from here.

"Solar is now the engine of the power transition," says Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford in the UK.

Solar has become the fastest-growing source of new electricity in history , and by far the largest source of new electricity globally. In 2025, it met three-quarters of the growth in the world's demand for electricity, overtaking wind power generation (wind power is also growing, just a little more slowly).

That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy – Dave Jones

"It wasn't expected," says Rosenow. Mainstream projections, he says, have underestimated solar year after year . Outlooks such as those from the International Energy Agency (IEA), an influential intergovernmental organisation based in Paris, "assumed linear growth and slowly falling costs, and got both wrong".

Over 2026, multiple sources indicate solar electricity generation will almost certainly far exceed nuclear globally. Nuclear's electricity generation has remained more or less constant since 2000, while solar's has increased some 2,700-fold.

Ember data shows solar electricity generation narrowly surpassing nuclear in 2025. In 2026, it will almost certainly well exceed it (Credit: Ember/BBC)

Solar, a mature technology for some 15 years now, became the cheapest electricity in history in 2020. Since then, solar has scaled, efficiency has risen, and the amount of silicon and silver used in panels has gone down, leading prices to fall yet further , says Jones.

"Massive Chinese manufacturing scale and current overcapacity have pushed module prices to record lows," says Rosenow.

In particular, a large fall in the price of panels in 2023-24 pushed us into the current era of what Jones calls "offensively cheap" solar. "A panel in itself is just so unbelievably cheap," he says. "It's well under $100 (£75)… and that's going to keep you generating electricity for 30, 40 years without any input at all."

Of course, it's not just in purely economic terms that solar is bringing down costs. Researchers have calculated the US's rising wind and solar generation brought it $249bn (£186bn) in climate and health benefits between 2019 and 2022 .

China is still the world's biggest solar power by far but is by no means the only player.

Despite the US imposing a variety of tariffs on solar , it remains the second country when it comes to installations, which are still skyrocketing – especially in states won by President Trump in 2024 . In fact, the US now has enough solar to power more than one-third of its households .

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Blaise Pascal invented fixed route public transport (2024)
items.content:
Blaise Pascal knew he was dying.  He was in his 30s and had been sick most of his life, but at least he didn’t have to worry about being forgotten.  He had already made transformative innovations in mathematics, physics, philosophy, and theology, and in his spare time he was assembling a collection of thoughts about God that would become the Pensées , which has been praised as some of the finest prose ever written in the French language.  He was fortunate to live at a time (the mid-1600s) when, if you were born to the right parents, nobody told you you needed to specialize.

So what did he do with the last lucid days of his life?  He invented fixed route public transport.

The vehicle used by Pascal’s service. Note that each had a fixed sign advertising the endpoints of the route. But who cares about the vehicle? What matters is the service.  Source: Taras Grescoe’s Substack .

Wikipedia currently says he invented the bus line, but that’s too narrow. Pascal’s network, which he called carrosses a cinq sols or “five penny carriages” used eight-passenger horse-drawn carriages, but they did what fixed route public transport does.  They operated predictable frequencies along multiple connecting routes, forming a network.  This is not just the ancestor of every city bus, but also of every train or tram.

Had this really not been done before?  Apparently not on land. Ferries are an ancient idea, both for crossing water bodies and for traveling along them.  They are fixed routes, of course, but that’s mostly because the shore is fixed.  Pascal’s idea was that even though carriages could go from anywhere to anywhere on Paris’s street network, a special kind of usefulness would arise if they didn’t do that, but instead followed paths that people could remember and plan around.

Here is the map of his complete network design:

Frequency ranged from 7.5 minutes to 15 minutes, so these came often enough that people could just go out and wait for them, not worrying about a schedule.  Their main failure was overcrowding and pass-ups, which of course is a kind of success.  Obviously, someone needed to invent a larger horse-drawn vehicle for this purpose, but that would wait a while still.  The first line began on March 18, 1662 and the whole network was operating by July, just before Pascal’s death, a pace of implementation that is hard to imagine today.  It’s likely that Pascal spent many of his final days thinking about this, when he wasn’t writing immortal prose about God.

Gazing at the map, I recognize many of the eternal principles of fixed route transit planning:  The lines try to remain far from each other, converging only on major destinations.  They are often perpendicular, which maximizes the odds that a connection between those routes will make lots of trips possible.  There are more or less straight lines running across the city — because where demand is spread uniformly, a straight line is more likely to match people’s desires than a winding one — and there’s an orbital line, yellow on the map, that goes all the way around the edge in a two way loop.  Orbitals are a common shape because they make such effective connections with radial lines, and their length means they connect an unusual number of origins and destinations directly.

At age 11, Pascal had re-derived much of Euclid’s geometry from scratch because his father kept the books from him, thinking he was still too young.  So, dying at 38, Pascal probably could sense that these principles were mathematically right, even though they’d never been written down before.

But as a network designer I wanted to know more.  How did this map come about?  Did Pascal ever explain the design himself? What explains the biggest exceptions to the principles?  The routes aren’t as straight as they could be.  And why do so many of the lines converge at Luxembourg Palace in the southwest?  Much of the government was around there, but still, was that really such a hub of citywide demand?  I…

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

Update 4: A new report suggests that Instagram accounts may be vulnerable to coordinated mass-report abuse. According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)
